title: Supramolecular Engineering to Improve Electrocatalytic CO2 Reduction Activity of Cu2O
abstract: Electrochemical conversion of CO2 into value-added fuels and feedstocks attracts worldwide attention to mitigate energy and environmental problems. However, pursuing highly efficient electrocatalyst is still a challenge. In this study, cuprous oxide (Cu2O) modified by cucurbit[6]urils (Q[6]), a kind of rigid macromolecule, is found to act as an efficient supramolecular inorganic nanocomposite catalyst for the electrochemical CO2 reduction reaction (CO2RR) to C1 fuels. This catalyst affords a high total faradaic efficiency (FECO+ formate) of 93.96% at a potential of 0.7 V vs. reversible hydrogen electrode and over 85% from 0.6 to 0.9 V in 0.5 M KHCO3, which is higher than that of pure Cu2O (39.89%). The enhancements in selectivity and activity for CO2RR could significantly benefit from the strong CO2 adsorption capacity and hydrophobic nature of the cavity of Q[6], which simultaneously trap gaseous reactants near the catalyst to tune the local environment and limit the diffusion of water molecules. This study provides a strategy to adjust catalytic environments through supramolecular engineering.

sections.heading: Supramolecular Engineering to Improve Electrocatalytic CO2 Reduction Activity of Cu2O
sections.text:
Ya Zhang,[a] Xiao-Yu Zhang,[a] Kai Chen,[b] and Wei-Yin Sun*[a]
Electrochemical conversion of CO2 into value-added fuels and feedstocks attracts worldwide attention to mitigate energy and environmental problems. However, pursuing highly efficient electrocatalyst is still a challenge. In this study, cuprous oxide (Cu2O) modified by cucurbit[6]urils (Q[6]), a kind of rigid macromolecule, is found to act as an efficient supramolecular inorganic nanocomposite catalyst for the electrochemical CO2 reduction reaction (CO2RR) to C1 fuels. This catalyst affords a high total faradaic efficiency (FECO+ formate) of 93.96% at a potential of 0.7 V vs. reversible hydrogen electrode and over 85% from 0.6 to 0.9 V in 0.5 M KHCO3, which is higher than that of pure Cu2O (39.89%). The enhancements in selectivity and activity for CO2RR could significantly benefit from the strong CO2 adsorption capacity and hydrophobic nature of the cavity of Q[6], which simultaneously trap gaseous reactants near the catalyst to tune the local environment and limit the diffusion of water molecules. This study provides a strategy to adjust catalytic environments through supramolecular engineering.
Transformation of carbon dioxide (CO2) into value-added chemicals and fuels is one of the most critical technological challenges of this century.[1,2] Electrochemical CO2 reduction reaction (CO2RR) is considered as a promising approach that can regenerate fuels from CO2 using electricity powered by abundant renewable source such as solar energy.[3,4] However, there are still challenges to overcome, such as the low electron affinity of CO2,
[5] low durability of electrocatalyst and competitive hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) in an aqueous solution.[6] Therefore, exploring an electrocatalyst with high
efficiency, selectivity and stability is still a crucial requirement to realize CO2RR.
Cu-based electrocatalysts exhibit unique capability in reducing CO2 to varied products like hydrocarbons, [7–9] alcohols,[10–12] formic acid/formate (depending on pH).[13,14] Various strategies have been adopted to improve the selectivity and activity of Cu-based electrocatalysts, for example introducing another metal to form bimetallic alloys,[15] tuning particle size,[16] modulating microstructure,[17] controlling surface facets[18] and using Cu single-atom catalyst.[19] However, HER is dominant in aqueous CO2RR systems, as it is kinetically more favorable than CO2RR.
[20,21] An effective way to improve the activity and selectivity of CO2RR is suppressing HER while increasing the local concentration of CO2 on the catalyst surface. [15]
Cucurbit[n]urils (Q[n]) as a new generation of macrocyclic molecules are made up of glycoluril units and have hydrophobic cavity.[22–25] The cavities of Q[n] are known to combine various small organic guests or gas molecules.[22] Q[6] particularly has an affinity for CO2 adsorption, which is comparable to metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) such as [Pd(2-pyrimidinolate)2]n and HKUST-1.
[26] CO2 can be adsorbed not only at the inner cavity of Q[6] but also externally to Q[6] molecules through hydrogen-bonding and dipole–quadrupole interactions with carbonyl portals.[22] Therefore, we propose a supramolecular engineering strategy to selectively tune the local chemical environment on the surface of electrocatalyst to suppress HER and facilitate CO2RR by fabricating supramolecular-inorganic nanocomposite.
Herein, we focus our attention on cuprous oxide (Cu2O) modified by Q[6] (Cu2O Q[6]) as an efficient catalyst towards conversion of CO2 into valuable chemicals. In 0.5 M KHCO3, this catalyst can reduce CO2 to CO and formate with a total faradaic efficiency (FECO+ formate) of 93.96% at potential of 0.7 V vs. reversible hydrogen electrode (RHE). It is worth noting that Q[6] plays an essential role in increasing the concentration of CO2 on the Cu2O surface and suppressing the competing HER compared with pure Cu2O.
The nanocomposite Cu2O Q[6] was prepared by a wet chemical method, in which Q[6] as a rigid macrocyclic compound with two identical portals is decorated on the surface of Cu2O (Figure 1a). First, the phase structures of asprepared Cu2O and Cu2O Q[6] were investigated by powder Xray diffraction (PXRD; see the Supporting Information, Figure S1). The peaks at 29.6, 36.5, 42.4, 61.5 and 73.7° can be well indexed to the (110), (111), (200), (220), and (311) planes of Cu2O (JCPDS No. 75-1531), respectively. Furthermore, the peaks shown in Figure 1b are also in good agreement with Cu2O and Q[6], demonstrating the synthesis of Cu2O Q[6]. Attenuated

Compared with the spectrum of pure Q[6], a redshift of approximately 7 cm 1 is observed for the carbonyl portal in Cu2O Q[6], indicating that the existence of interactions between Cu2O and Q[6].
[27] The morphological features of the as-prepared samples were investigated by scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and transmission electron microscope (TEM). The SEM image (Figure 1d) reveals that the final obtained Cu2O Q[6] has a near-spherical nanostructure. The TEM image (Figure 1e) further suggests that Cu2O nanoparticles are uniformly distributed in the Cu2O Q[6] composite. Compared with pure Cu2O (Figure S2), the presence of Q[6] contributes to the formation of small nanoparticles. High-resolution TEM (HRTEM) image (Figure 1f) shows lattice fringes with an interplane spacing of 0.245 nm, corresponding to the (111) plane of Cu2O phase. In addition, some lattice fringes are blurred (orange box in Figure 1f), which is caused by the surface modification of Q[6]. We also performed high angle annular dark field scanning transmission electron microscopy
(HAADF-STEM) and energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) mapping. Figure 1g shows HAADF-STEM image of Cu2O Q[6] composite. The overlay map (Figure 1h) and elemental mapping images (Figure 1i) indicate the uniform distribution of Cu, O, C and N elements in Cu2O Q[6]. The molar ratio of Q[6] to Cu2O in the Cu2O Q[6] nanocomposite is 0.18 :1 estimated by energy dispersive X-ray (EDX).
X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) was employed to investigate the surface chemical composition of Cu2O Q[6] and Cu2O (Figure 2). The XPS survey spectrum of Cu2O Q[6] (Figure 2a) clearly confirms the presence of C, N, O, and Cu. Furthermore, no N is found in the XPS survey spectrum of Cu2O (Figure S3a). In the high-resolution Cu2p spectrum (Figure 2b and Figure S3b), the peaks at 932.2 and 952.3 eV can be attributed to Cu2p3/2 and Cu2p1/2, respectively, and the corresponding species is Cu+ or Cu0.[28] The Cu state identification was further determined by Cu LMM Auger spectra due to the binding energies of Cu+ and Cu0 states are too resemble to be distinguished.[29] The peak at the kinetic energy of 916.4 eV

[30] The high-resolution C1s and N1s spectra of Cu2O Q[6] originate from Q[6]. The deconvoluted C1s spectrum (Figure 2c) shows peaks at 284.7, 287.1, and 288.7 eV, attributed to C in C H, C N, and C=O, respectively.[31] And the N1s signal with a binding energy of 399.7 eV (Figure 2d) corresponds to the C N bond of Q[6].[27] All of the above observations certainly support the formation of Cu2O Q[6].
The CO2RR performance of the catalyst was first investigated in 0.5 M KHCO3 solution using an H-type three-electrode cell. The linear sweep voltammograms (LSVs) curves over the Cu2O Q[6] under CO2-saturated electrolyte solution present a higher cathodic current density than that generated in N2saturated electrolyte (Figure 3a), revealing the occurrence of CO2RR. To further explore the catalytic performances for CO2 reduction, we carried out chronoamperometric tests, and the gas and liquid products were detected by online gas chromatography (GC) and 1H NMR. The chronoamperometry curves (Figure S5) of Cu2O Q[6] at different applied potentials reveal good electrochemical stability during the CO2RR tests. The reduction current generated in the initial 10 s comes from the reduction of Cu2O (Figure S5b).
[32] CO and H2 as the major gas reduction products were detected by GC (Figure S6), and the liquid products were identified by 1H NMR (Figure S7). As shown in Figure 3b and Table S1, Cu2O Q[6] displays a maximum total faradaic efficiency (FECO+ formate) of 93.96% at 0.7 V vs. RHE. Importantly, the total FEs of CO and formate remain over 85.00% at potentials ranging from 0.6 to 0.9 V. However, the total FEs of CO2 reduction for pure Cu2O is only 39.89% (Figure S8 and Table S2) at 0.7 V. Furthermore, the FEs of H2
for Cu2O Q[6] at different potentials are much lower than that of pure Cu2O (Figure 3c), implying that the introduction of Q[6] suppresses HER. The total current densities of CO2 reduction and HER at different potentials are calculated to gain a deeper understanding of the CO2RR activity for the as-prepared catalyst. The partial current densities for CO2RR in Cu2O Q[6] with presence of Q[6] remains higher than that of pure Cu2O (Figure 3d). On the contrary, it is interesting to note that the jH2 (Figure S9) shows an opposite trend to the partial current densities for CO2RR, revealing that the hydrophobic nature of the cavity of Q[6] decreases the usability of water molecules and resultantly suppresses HER. Meanwhile, the modification of Q[6] limits the diffusion of water molecules, which can further change the concentration profiles of CO2.
[33] The results further distinctly certify that Q[6] in the Cu2O Q[6] composite plays a crucial role in suppressing HER and enhancing the selectivity and activity of CO2RR.
To explore the influence of the Q[6] loading, we tested the catalytic performances of Cu2O with different loading amount of Q[6]. The total FEs of CO and formate increase from 0 to 0.2 mmol and then drop a little (Figure S10). However, the partial current densities for CO2RR with different loading amount of Q[6] at 0.7 V increase firstly, then decrease rapidly. A moderate amount of Q[6] can thus enhance the CO2RR activity and excessive Q[6] may over-suppress the availability of electrolyte and protons for CO2RR. [34]
The strong adsorption capacity of the catalyst for CO2 not only improves the local concentration of CO2 and accelerates mass transport on the surface of the catalyst but also facilitates the electroreduction of CO2 to useful products. [28,35,36] The CO2

A higher CO2 adsorption capacity in Cu2O Q[6] (Figure 4a) is ascribed to the presence of Q[6] with abundant cavities to uptake CO2 molecules. Fluorescent dye displacement measurements were performed to further verify the binding of CO2 with Cu2O Q[6] experimentally. In this method, trans-4[4(dimethylamino)styryl]-1-methylpyridinium (DSMI) was used as an indicator dye and we utilized the fluorescence of the host-

As illustrated in Figure 4b, Cu2O ·DSMI exhibits no fluorescence. However, the complexed state of Q[6] ·DSMI and Cu2O Q[6] ·DSMI display strong fluorescence and then decrease after CO2 injection for 10 min, implying that Q[6] does exist in the compound of Cu2O Q[6] and the cavity of Q[6] is not occupied. Moreover, CO2 as guest can enter into the cavity of Q[6] and has strong interactions with Q[6]. Furthermore, the contact angles of water on the surface of Cu2O Q[6] and Cu2O were measured to evaluate the hydrophobicity of the catalysts. As shown in Figure S11, Cu2O Q[6] electrode exhibits a contact angle of 139.5° and 124.0° before and after the electrolysis, which are larger than those of pure Cu2O, indicating that the introduction of Q[6] can indeed enhance the hydrophobicity nature of Cu2O.
To further confirm the role of Q[6] in the CO2RR, we measured the electrochemical active surface area (ECSA). As depicted in Figure S12 and Figure 4c, the double-layer capacitance of Cu2O Q[6] is bigger than that of Cu2O, implying a higher electrochemical active surface area and more exposed active sites due to the formation of smaller nanoparticles in the presence of Q[6], which is beneficial to enhance the activity of the catalyst.[39] All of the above results evidently indicate that the introduction of Q[6] significantly enhances the CO2 adsorption capacity for Cu2O Q[6] by strong interactions with CO2 and simultaneously tunes the local chemical environment around the Cu2O surface. To a certain extent, it can also prevent Cu2O from the contact with electrolyte, thus inhibiting the HER process.[28] Therefore, Cu2O Q[6] acts as an efficient catalyst for the electrocatalytic reduction of CO2 to C1 fuels with significantly suppressed HER.
Since stability is a crucial parameter for evaluating the catalyst, the stability of catalyst was examined. Figure 4d displays that the FECO+ formate of Cu2O Q[6] has no significant attenuation during six consecutive CO2RR tests for every two hours. In addition, the current density for the 24 h long-term test remains stable at 0.7 V under sustained CO2 gas flow in the cathode (Figure S13). The change of valence for Cu2O during the CO2RR may occur as reported previously,
[40,41] the surface Cu2O can be reduced to metallic copper during CO2 reduction and then reoxidized to Cu2O after the cathodic potential is removed. After the CO2RR, the morphology of the electrocatalyst is remained (Figure S14), and the PXRD pattern of Cu2O Q[6] barely changes (Figure S15). Moreover, XPS was used to study the valence state of Cu after the durability test, and the samples were stored and transferred in a vacuumsealed package before measurement to reduce the change of the surface. We can still observe the existence of C, N, O and Cu elements as shown in Figure S16. And the valence state of Cu is still maintaining at Cu+ state, indicating that the composites are still Cu2O in nature (Figure S17). These results imply that Cu2O Q[6] has enough electrochemical and structural stability during CO2RR.
In summary, we developed the composite Cu2O Q[6] by surface supramolecular engineering as an efficient CO2RR electrocatalyst to convert CO2 into C1 fuels. It gave a maximum
FECO+ formate of 93.96% at 0.7 V and over 85.00% from 0.6 to 0.9 V, which is much higher than that of pure Cu2O. Q[6] endows this composite with a significantly enhanced CO2 adsorption capacity and hydrophobicity, which improves the activity and selectivity of CO2RR and suppresses HER by simultaneously tuning the local chemical environment around the Cu2O surface and reducing the availability of water molecules. This study will open up new ways to develop supramolecular inorganic composites for the CO2RR.

sections.heading: Reagents and materials
sections.text: Copper(II) sulfate pentahydrate (CuSO4 ·5H2O), sodium hydroxide (NaOH), L-ascorbic acid and potassium bicarbonate (KHCO3) were purchased from Aladdin Industrial Corporation. All chemicals were purchased commercially and used as received without further purification. Ultrapure water, which was purified with a Millipore system, was used throughout the experiments.

sections.heading: Catalyst synthesis
sections.text: In a typical synthetic process, CuSO4 ·5H2O (250 mg, 1 mmol) and Q[6] (0.2 mmol) were dissolved in 0.1 m aqueous NaOH (20 mL) solution. The solution became a light blue suspension. Next, lascorbic acid (176 mg, 1 mmol) was added into the suspension under vigorous stirring and the suspension was stirred for 20 min at room temperature. The solid product Cu2O Q[6] was obtained by centrifugation. It was washed alternately with ethanol and deionized water, and then dried in a vacuum oven at 50 °C. Cu2O was obtained under identical conditions without the addition of Q[6]. Cu2O Q[6]-0.1, Cu2O Q[6]-0.3, and Cu2O Q[6]-0.4 were obtained under identical conditions with the addition of 0.1, 0.3, and 0.4 mmol Q[6], respectively.
